issues.subcategory: Implausible chi-square difference test value
issues.description: The chi-square difference test comparing the cross-lagged effects of SDO→RWA and RWA→SDO yields Δχ²(1) = 15,389.13, which is extraordinarily large for a single degree-of-freedom test comparing two small unstandardized path coefficients (B = .02 vs. B = -.001). This value is orders of magnitude larger than the other chi-square difference tests reported (e.g., 50.98 and 39.97) and raises serious concerns about a computational error, misspecification, or reporting mistake. Such an extreme value warrants verification.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001)

issues.subcategory: Cross-lagged panel model limitations for causal inference
issues.description: The authors use a traditional autoregressive cross-lagged panel model (CLPM) and interpret results as evidence for causal pathways. However, the traditional CLPM conflates between-person and within-person effects, meaning that the cross-lagged coefficients may reflect stable between-person differences rather than within-person change processes. More appropriate models such as the Random Intercept Cross-Lagged Panel Model (RI-CLPM; Hamaker et al., 2015) would separate these components and provide more defensible causal inferences. The authors' causal language ('causal pathway,' 'causal effect') is therefore not well supported by the analytic approach.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism.

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming causality from observational longitudinal data
issues.description: Throughout the discussion, the authors make causal claims (e.g., 'causal pathway,' 'causal effect,' 'the desire to dominate leads to lower environmentalism') based on cross-lagged panel analysis of observational data. Even with longitudinal data, cross-lagged models cannot establish causality due to potential unmeasured confounders, and the traditional CLPM is particularly limited in this regard. The abstract similarly states 'the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance,' implying causation.
issues.quote: this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes

issues.subcategory: Narrow operationalization of environmentalism
issues.description: Environmentalism is operationalized using only two items measuring willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. This is a very narrow measure that captures only behavioral sacrifice intentions, not broader environmental attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors. The authors frequently discuss 'environmentalism,' 'environmental attitudes,' and 'climate change denial' interchangeably in the introduction and discussion, but the measure does not capture these broader constructs. This creates a mismatch between the constructs discussed and what was actually measured.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual's willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] two items on sacrifice intentions

issues.subcategory: Missing item-level details for RWA across time points
issues.description: The authors note that one RWA item was not assessed at Time 2 but was included at all other time points. This means the RWA measure had different numbers of items across time points (5 items at T2 vs. 6 at other times). The authors do not explain how this was handled in the latent variable specification, whether factor loading constraints were adjusted, or what impact this might have on measurement invariance testing and the validity of the longitudinal comparisons.
issues.quote: The item "Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done", was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.subcategory: Poor model fit accepted with insufficient justification
issues.description: The CFI of .86 is below the conventional threshold of .90 (and well below the more stringent .95 threshold). The authors dismiss this by attributing it to model complexity, but poor CFI can also indicate model misspecification. The justification for accepting the model based solely on RMSEA and SRMR while ignoring CFI is insufficient. Furthermore, the RMSEA confidence interval is reported as [.025, .026], which is implausibly narrow and appears to be an error (the point estimate of .03 falls outside this CI).
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07)

issues.subcategory: RMSEA point estimate outside its own confidence interval
issues.description: The RMSEA is reported as .03 with a 90% CI of [.025, .026]. The point estimate of .03 falls outside the reported confidence interval, which is mathematically impossible. Either the point estimate or the confidence interval (or both) are incorrectly reported.

issues.subcategory: Missing sample sizes per time point and attrition details
issues.description: The authors report 22,974 total participants but do not provide the number of participants at each of the five time points, nor do they report attrition rates across waves. For a five-year longitudinal study, understanding how many participants completed each wave is critical for evaluating the validity of the findings and the appropriateness of FIML for handling missing data.
issues.quote: Of the 22,974 participants included in this study, the average age was 43 years at Time 1

issues.subcategory: No analysis of attrition patterns or MCAR/MAR assumptions
issues.description: The authors use FIML to handle missing data but do not report the extent of missing data, whether missingness patterns were examined, or whether the data meet the MAR assumption required for FIML to produce unbiased estimates. In a five-year panel study, systematic attrition (e.g., participants with extreme ideological views dropping out) could bias results even with FIML.
issues.quote: Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.subcategory: Reporting SD instead of SE for parameter estimates
issues.description: The authors report 'SD' alongside unstandardized path coefficients (e.g., B = .83, SD = .01). In structural equation modeling output, the value accompanying parameter estimates is typically the standard error (SE), not the standard deviation. This appears to be a reporting error that could confuse readers attempting to evaluate or replicate the findings.
issues.quote: the autoregressive path for willingness to sacrifice was strong (B = .83, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [.82, .84])

issues.subcategory: Stationarity assumption not tested
issues.description: The authors impose a stationary model where all cross-lagged parameters are constrained to be equal across time points. While they justify this by stating they are interested in 'overall and comparative effects,' they do not test whether the stationarity assumption holds by comparing the constrained model to an unconstrained model. If the effects change over time (e.g., strengthening or weakening), the stationary model could mask important dynamics and produce misleading average estimates.
issues.quote: We imposed this stationary cross-lagged model because we were more interested in the overall and comparative effects of SDO and RWA on changes in environmentalism, and not on whether these effects change during the interval measured.

issues.subcategory: Abbreviated scales with low reliability
issues.description: Both SDO and RWA were measured with only 6 items from their full scales, yielding reliabilities of .69 and .70 respectively. While the authors acknowledge this, these low reliabilities can attenuate cross-lagged effects and bias comparisons between predictors. The use of latent variables partially addresses this, but the small number of indicators per construct limits the ability to model measurement error adequately.
issues.quote: Reliabilities for SDO and RWA were poorer than is typically the case when the full scales are used, but are consistent with expectations based on previous research using short measures

issues.subcategory: Contradiction between predictions and findings on SDO-RWA relationship
issues.description: The authors predicted reciprocal cross-time effects between SDO and RWA based on Duckitt's theorizing about New Zealand's polarized political system. However, they found only a unidirectional effect (RWA→SDO). In the discussion, they explain this by citing Duckitt et al.'s [23] argument about authoritarian-conservative societies showing non-significant SDO→RWA paths. This post-hoc explanation contradicts their initial prediction and the reasoning behind it (that NZ's polarized system would produce bidirectional effects).
issues.quote: Duckitt suggests that RWA and SDO exhibit positive bidirectional associations over time... This contradicted our initial expectations, however it is consistent with Duckitt et al. [23]

issues.subcategory: Overclaiming generalizability from single-country sample
issues.description: The authors claim their results are 'highly generalisable' based on a nationally representative New Zealand sample. However, New Zealand has a unique sociopolitical context (as the authors themselves note regarding SDO-RWA correlations), and the relationship between ideology and environmentalism may differ across cultural contexts. The claim of high generalizability is overstated.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.subcategory: FIML described as imputation
issues.description: The authors describe FIML (Full Information Maximum Likelihood) as imputing missing data. FIML does not impute missing values; rather, it estimates parameters using all available data by maximizing the likelihood function for each case's observed data pattern. This is a conceptual mischaracterization of the method.
issues.quote: Missing data were imputed using FIML.

issues.subcategory: No descriptive statistics for later time points
issues.description: Descriptive statistics and correlations are only presented for Time 1. Given that this is a five-wave longitudinal study, descriptive statistics (means, SDs, correlations, and reliabilities) for all time points would be important for evaluating trends, potential ceiling/floor effects, and changes in measurement properties over time.
issues.quote: Table 1 presents the descriptive statistics and correlations between our variables at Time 1.

issues.subcategory: No pre-registration mentioned
issues.description: There is no mention of pre-registration for this study. Given the multiple analytic decisions involved (choice of model constraints, significance threshold, which fit indices to prioritize, how to handle the missing RWA item), pre-registration would help address concerns about researcher degrees of freedom. The post-hoc nature of some interpretations (e.g., the SDO-RWA finding) further highlights this concern.

issues.subcategory: No control variables included
issues.description: The model does not include any demographic or socioeconomic control variables (e.g., age, gender, education, income, political affiliation) that could confound the relationships between SDO, RWA, and environmentalism. Given that these variables are known to relate to both ideology and environmental attitudes, their omission weakens causal inferences.

issues.subcategory: Conflation of environmentalism constructs in discussion
issues.description: The discussion extensively discusses climate change denial, environmental racism, environmental inequality, and speciesism, but the study only measured willingness to make personal sacrifices for the environment. The theoretical implications drawn go far beyond what the measured construct can support. For example, linking findings to environmental racism and the hierarchy enforcement hypothesis requires measures of support for environmental exploitation or acceptance of environmental inequality, not just sacrifice willingness.
issues.quote: Our findings therefore highlight Social Dominant's way of thinking as having the potential to exacerbate environmental inequality

issues.subcategory: Missing measurement invariance testing details
issues.description: The authors describe constraining factor loadings, intercepts, and residual variances to equality across time points, which constitutes strict measurement invariance. However, they do not report the results of sequential measurement invariance tests (configural, metric, scalar, strict) to demonstrate that these constraints are tenable. Imposing strict invariance without testing whether it holds could mask measurement non-invariance and bias results.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the factor loadings of our latent variables to equality... Next, we constrained the means (intercepts) of the factors to equality... We also constrained to equality the residual variance for the same item over time

issues.subcategory: Inconsistency between abstract and results on RWA significance
issues.description: The abstract states 'RWA was a weaker, but significant, negative predictor,' which is consistent with the results (p = .001). However, the introduction reviews literature suggesting RWA effects disappear when SDO is controlled, and the study uses a conservative p < .01 threshold. The RWA effect (B = -.02) is very small and barely meets the conservative threshold, yet the abstract and conclusion present it as a clear finding without noting its marginal nature relative to the adopted threshold.

issues.subcategory: Latent variable specification details missing
issues.description: The environmentalism construct is measured with only two items. With only two indicators, the latent variable is not identified without additional constraints. The authors do not discuss how identification was achieved for this construct, which is important for evaluating the model specification.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as individual's willingness to make sacrifices for the environment. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] two items

issues.subcategory: Unequal time intervals not addressed
issues.description: The study spans five annual waves (2009-2013), but the authors do not confirm that the intervals between waves are approximately equal for all participants. If there is variation in when participants completed surveys across waves, the stationarity assumption and interpretation of cross-lagged effects could be affected.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated in the first five years of the project (from 2009 to 2013).
